_meta: A dependency whose capacity changes between a healthy and a degraded regime, used to show why a STATIC in-flight concurrency limit is wrong in at least one regime -- too high overloads a degraded dependency, too low starves a healthy one -- and why an adaptive concurrency limit (an AIMD controller driven by latency) tracks the dependency's current capacity and is right in both. A concurrency limit caps how many requests a client keeps in flight to a dependency at once; it is the client-side analogue of a bulkhead. The dependency has a capacity C -- the number of concurrent requests it serves at its baseline latency d0. Send more than C at once and the excess queues, so latency rises roughly in proportion to how far concurrency exceeds capacity (Little's law); send fewer than C and you leave throughput on the table. The problem is that C is not fixed: a dependency that normally serves 10 concurrent requests may, when degraded (a slow database, a GC pause, a downstream outage), serve only 2. A static limit chosen for the healthy regime overloads the degraded one; a static limit chosen for the degraded regime wastes capacity in the healthy one. An adaptive limit adjusts continuously -- additive-increase while latency is at baseline, multiplicative-decrease when latency spikes, like TCP congestion control -- so it converges to the current C. d0 is the baseline latency; threshold is the latency at or below which the controller increases; regimes gives each regime's capacity C; static_high and static_low are two fixed limits. All of these are the fixture; the latency and throughput of each policy in each regime, and the limit the AIMD controller converges to, are computed.
